articles.title: File descriptors
articles.summary: Unix's basic communication channels: stdin, stdout, and stderr

blocks.content: When a process starts on Unix/Linux, the operating system automatically assigns it numbered communication channels called file descriptors (FDs). They're simply integers that represent an open connection — it could be to a file, to the screen, to the keyboard, to a network, or to another process.
Three of those channels come assigned by default in every process, always, with no exceptions:

items.title: stdin (FD 0)
items.body: Standard Input. What goes into the process. By default it comes from the keyboard. The process reads it when it needs input.

items.title: stdout (FD 1)
items.body: Standard Output. The process's normal output. By default it goes to the screen. It's where the process writes its results.

items.title: stderr (FD 2)
items.body: Standard Error. Errors and diagnostic messages. Also goes to the screen by default, but it's a separate channel.

blocks.content: They're channels, not files. You can redirect them wherever you want. The process doesn't know or care whether it's reading from the keyboard or from a file — either way it reads from FD 0. That abstraction is what makes the whole system so flexible.

Why are there two output channels (stdout and stderr)? Because mixing normal output with errors is a problem. If your script produces useful data on stdout and an error on stderr, whoever processes the output can ignore the errors without them contaminating the data.

articles.title: stdin, stdout, stderr in action
articles.summary: Each channel has a well-defined role and a convention everyone follows

blocks.label: example-script.sh
blocks.content:
#!/bin/bash
# Read from stdin (FD 0)
read -r INPUT
# Write to stdout (FD 1) — normal output
echo "Processed: $INPUT"
# Write to stderr (FD 2) — errors only
echo "Something went wrong" >&2
`>&2` is how you tell the shell "send this to file descriptor 2 instead of 1." Without that suffix, echo always writes to stdout.

blocks.label: terminal
blocks.content:
./script.sh 2>/dev/null           # discard stderr, show only stdout
./script.sh 1>/dev/null           # discard stdout, show only stderr
./script.sh 2>&1                  # combine stderr into stdout to see them together

articles.title: Pipes: connecting processes
articles.summary: A pipe (|) connects one process's stdout to the next one's stdin

blocks.label: terminal
blocks.content:
echo "hello world"
# without a pipe: echo writes to the screen

echo "hello world" | wc -w
# with a pipe: echo's stdout → wc's stdin
# result: 2

echo '{"name":"John"}' | jq '.name'
# the same happens with JSON
# result: "John"
The pipe is **synchronous** — the second process waits on the first. Data flows as a continuous stream, not as a file that's written and then read later.

This is exactly what Claude Code does with hooks. Claude Code is 'Process A' — it builds a JSON with the event context and writes it to stdout. Your hook is 'Process B' — it receives it via stdin, does something with it, and writes its response to stdout. Claude Code reads that response and makes a decision.

articles.title: Exit codes: result signals
articles.summary: The exit code is how a process communicates success or failure

blocks.content: When a process ends, it leaves a number for the process that called it. That number is the exit code. In Unix, the convention is universal: **0 means success**, any other number means some kind of failure. The range is 0-255.

items.title: exit 0
items.body: Success. The process finished without issues. Claude Code parses stdout looking for control JSON.

items.title: exit 1
items.body: Generic error. Unix convention for failure. In Claude Code it's a non-blocking error — it continues but shows a notice.

items.title: exit 2
items.body: Active block. Specific to Claude Code. A 'stop the action' signal. stdout is ignored and stderr is passed to Claude.

blocks.content: exit 1 is the Unix convention for 'something failed,' but in Claude Code it **blocks nothing**. Only exit 2 blocks. If you want to prevent Claude from executing something, you have to use exit 2 explicitly — exit 1 simply logs an error and moves on.

articles.title: How Claude Code calls hooks
articles.summary: The full mechanism of stdin, stdout, stderr, and exit codes in action

items.title: Builds the context JSON
items.body: Claude Code constructs a JSON object with all the relevant event information: what happened, which tool was called, what arguments it has, the session_id, the cwd, etc.

items.title: Launches the hook process
items.body: Runs the command defined in the config — it can be a bash script, a Python binary, any executable. Launches it as a child process.

items.title: Writes the JSON to the hook's stdin
items.body: The JSON is written directly to FD 0 (stdin) of the hook process. The hook reads it with cat, jq, sys.stdin in Python, etc.

items.title: Waits for the hook to finish
items.body: Claude Code blocks and waits. The hook has a configured timeout (600s by default). If it exceeds the timeout, Claude Code kills the process.

items.title: Reads the exit code
items.body: When the hook finishes, Claude Code reads its exit code. This determines what to do with stdout and stderr next.

items.title: Processes stdout and stderr based on exit code
items.body: Exit 0: parses stdout as control JSON. Exit 2: ignores stdout, takes stderr and passes it to Claude as the reason for the block.

blocks.content: Let's see exactly what happens when Claude tries to run `rm -rf /tmp` and a hook is configured.

blocks.label: What Claude Code writes to the hook's stdin
guard.sh
blocks.content:
#!/bin/bash
# Read everything that arrived on stdin
INPUT=$(cat /dev/stdin)

# Extract the command from the JSON with jq
CMD=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.tool_input.command')

# rm -rf is dangerous → block it
if echo "$CMD" | grep -q 'rm -rf'; then
  # Write to stderr — this is what Claude will see
  echo "rm -rf blocked by security policy" >&2
  # Exit 2 → Claude Code knows it must block
  exit 2
fi

# No problems → exit 0, normal flow
exit 0
Claude receives the hook's stderr and processes it as a system error. Claude understands it and responds:

blocks.label: What Claude sees
blocks.content:
Error: rm -rf blocked by security policy

Claude adjusts its behavior: "I can't run that
command because it's blocked by a security policy.
Would you like me to look for a safer alternative?"

From Claude's perspective, when a hook blocks something with exit 2, it's as if the operating system had returned an error. Claude **doesn't distinguish** between 'the hook blocked it' and 'the command failed on its own.' The hook's stderr becomes the error message Claude processes.

articles.title: Redirections: fine control over channels
articles.summary: Redirecting stdin, stdout, and stderr to files or other destinations

blocks.label: terminal
blocks.content:
./script.sh > output.txt                    # redirect stdout to a file
./script.sh >> output.txt                   # append (don't overwrite)
./script.sh 2> errores.txt                  # redirect stderr to a file
./script.sh 2> /dev/null                    # discard stderr
./script.sh 2>&1                            # combine stderr into stdout
./script.sh < input.json                    # feed stdin from a file
./script.sh < input.json > output.txt 2>/dev/null  # all together
`2>&1` is read literally as 'redirect FD 2 to the same destination as FD 1.' The `&` indicates that what follows is a file descriptor, not a file name.

When Claude Code launches your hook, internally it's doing something equivalent to `echo "$JSON" | ./your-hook.sh` but capturing stdout and stderr separately — it doesn't combine them. That's why you can write to stderr with `>&2` for error messages and to stdout for the response JSON, and Claude Code treats them differently.

articles.title: jq: processing JSON from shell
articles.summary: The essential tool for working with JSON in hooks

blocks.content: Hooks receive and emit JSON. In bash, the standard tool for reading and building JSON is **jq**. It's nearly mandatory for writing hooks.

blocks.label: Read the full JSON
blocks.content: INPUT=$(cat /dev/stdin)

blocks.label: Extract fields with -r (raw)
blocks.content:
TOOL=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.tool_name')
CMD=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.tool_input.command // empty')
# The // empty avoids the variable ending up with the string 'null'

blocks.label: Build response JSON
blocks.content: jq -n '{ "hookSpecificOutput": { "hookEventName": "PreToolUse", "permissionDecision": "deny" } }'

blocks.label: Build JSON with bash variables
blocks.content:
jq -n \
  --arg reason "Command blocked: $CMD" \
  '{ "hookSpecificOutput": { "hookEventName": "PreToolUse", "permissionDecision": "deny", "permissionDecisionReason": $reason } }'

items.title: -r (raw output)
items.body: Without -r, jq prints strings with quotes: "hello". With -r, it prints plain: hello. To assign to bash variables, always use -r.

items.title: -n (null input)
items.body: Without -n, jq expects input on stdin. With -n, it builds JSON from scratch without reading stdin. Ideal for generating responses.

items.title: --arg
items.body: --arg name value injects a bash variable into jq as a string. Avoids escaping issues when building JSON with dynamic values.

blocks.content: If the hook is a Python script, `import json, sys` and `data = json.load(sys.stdin)` does exactly the same thing as `cat /dev/stdin | jq`. Python is more convenient for complex logic — the stdin/stdout/exit code mechanism is identical.

articles.title: Streams, buffers, and why they matter
articles.summary: Subtle details about how data flows between processes

subsections.title: The difference between a stream and a file

blocks.content: Data on stdin doesn't all arrive at once like a file — it arrives as a **stream**. You can start reading it before it's finished arriving.

When you run `cat /dev/stdin` in a hook, you're telling the system 'read all of stdin until it closes.' Claude Code writes the complete JSON and closes the pipe — at that point cat returns with all the data.

subsections.title: How to read stdin in different languages

blocks.label: Bash: read it all at once (recommended)
blocks.content:
INPUT=$(cat)              # cat with no args = cat /dev/stdin
INPUT=$(cat /dev/stdin)   # equivalent, more explicit

blocks.label: Bash: read line by line
blocks.content:
while IFS= read -r line; do
  echo "$line"
done

blocks.label: Python: read it all
blocks.content:
import json, sys
data = json.load(sys.stdin)   # parses directly from the stream

blocks.label: Node.js: read it all

blocks.content: If you use `read -r INPUT` instead of `INPUT=$(cat)`, you only read the **first line** of stdin. Claude Code's JSON can be multiline or very long — you'd lose everything that doesn't fit on the first line. Always use `$(cat)` or `$(cat /dev/stdin)` to read the complete JSON.

When your hook writes to stdout, the system may buffer the data before sending it to Claude Code. In most cases this doesn't matter because the process ends and the buffer flushes. But if your hook writes output and then hangs, Claude Code might not see anything until the hook finishes.

blocks.label: Python: force a flush
blocks.content: print(json.dumps(response), flush=True)

blocks.label: Bash: no problem
blocks.content: echo '{"continue": true}'  # echo always flushes automatically

articles.title: Environment variables and working directory
articles.summary: What context your hook receives when Claude Code runs it

subsections.title: The environment variables Claude Code injects

items.title: CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR
items.body: Current project directory. Example: /home/user/mi-proyecto

items.title: CLAUDE_SESSION_ID
items.body: Unique session identifier. Example: abc123def456

items.title: CLAUDE_TRANSCRIPT_PATH
items.body: Path to the transcript file. You can read the transcript for historical context.

blocks.content: The hook's cwd is the project directory (the same as CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR). You can run `git status` or `npm test` directly without navigating there first — you're already in the right place.

blocks.label: Count tool calls in the session
blocks.content: grep -c '"type":"tool_use"' "$CLAUDE_TRANSCRIPT_PATH"

blocks.label: View the last 3 events
blocks.content: tail -3 "$CLAUDE_TRANSCRIPT_PATH" | jq '.'

blocks.label: Extract all bash commands
blocks.content:
jq -r 'select(.type=="tool_use" and .name=="Bash") | .input.command' \
  "$CLAUDE_TRANSCRIPT_PATH"

blocks.label: In Python
blocks.content:
import json, os
path = os.environ['CLAUDE_TRANSCRIPT_PATH']
events = [json.loads(l) for l in open(path)]

articles.title: How HTTP hooks work
articles.summary: HTTP hooks use a different mechanism but the contract is the same

blocks.content: HTTP-type hooks don't launch a process — they make an HTTP POST. Instead of connecting stdin/stdout between processes, Claude Code serializes the event context as a JSON body and sends it to your endpoint. The server responds with the same JSON format a command hook would return.

subsections.title: Mapping status codes to exit codes

items.title: HTTP 200
items.body: Equivalent to exit 0. The response body is parsed as control JSON. The permissionDecision, additionalContext, etc. fields work the same way.

items.title: HTTP 4xx / 5xx
items.body: Equivalent to a non-zero exit. Non-blocking error. The body is treated as stderr — shown as a notice in the transcript but execution continues.

blocks.content: HTTP hooks are the only ones that can exfiltrate data off your machine. That's why `allowedHttpHookUrls` in managed settings lets you restrict which URLs they can connect to. A malicious HTTP hook could send the contents of your files to an external server — exactly the kind of attack you want to prevent in team environments.
